scenario: Today's systems track is less about whether the model itself is fast enough, and more about repeated work, idle time, and skew on the serving path. Wide-beam generative retrieval folds identifier constraints into a model-native output path, and closed-loop throughput can be several times a custom processor baseline. Multi-vector retrieval uses one data-aware graph index to approximate MaxSim mainly on CPU. Recommender user profiles are stored as reusable KV cache so ranking calls need not re-prefill every time, and skewed event streams are resplit at checkpoints so the busiest worker no longer runs far above the mean. Gains from speculative decoding change with hardware, concurrency, and modality, which calls for hardware-aware search, visual head routing, and preemption that waits until a request is nearly done. Reinforcement-learning rollout still needs migration and early stop to cut tail bubbles, and token-level routing needs a serving system that can actually carry the algorithmic gain, just as a public backend on new chips needs the runtime and cache hierarchy first.

papers.title: Efficient Wide-Beam Generative Retrieval with Model-Native Trie Decoding and Shared-Context Attention
papers.authors: Vedant Jhaveri, Arashpreet Singh Mor, Satyam Kumar, Alex Tsun, Qing Lan, Shaunak Mishra, Sriram Vasudevan
papers.abstract: Generative retrieval (GR) predicts catalog entries as short semantic identifiers (SIDs). Trie-constrained beam search keeps these identifiers valid, but wide beams expose two serving costs: vocabulary-wide score tensors that are mostly discarded, and repeated attention over the same prompt. We present Trie-Head, a model-native output interface that stores the identifier trie as validated GPU tensors. Compared with a Python custom logit processor (CLP), it reduces CPU--GPU coordination and memory traffic by avoiding Python constraint callbacks and vocabulary-wide candidate buffers. It scores compact codebook candidates and streams the full-vocabulary normalizer, preserving the original model's valid-token scores in real arithmetic without retraining. Shared-context attention complements this output path by reusing prompt key/value blocks across beams while preserving their private decode tails. We implement both mechanisms in SGLang and evaluate candidate sourcing for LinkedIn Hiring Assistant and qualification retrieval for the Qualification Retrieval Platform. The combined system improves closed-loop throughput by up to 5.57x over the CLP baseline and up to 2.63x over BF16 FlashRec at a common beam width of 200 on the Qualification Retrieval Platform workload.
papers.summary: Generative retrieval maps requests to catalog entries as short semantic IDs, and trie-constrained beam search keeps those IDs valid, but wide beams create two serving costs: vocabulary-wide score tensors that are mostly discarded, and repeated attention over the same prompt. A model-native output interface stores the identifier trie as validated GPU tensors, avoiding Python constraint callbacks and vocabulary-wide candidate buffers. It scores compact codebook candidates and streams the full-vocabulary normalizer, preserving the original model's valid-token scores in real arithmetic without retraining. Shared-context attention reuses prompt key-value blocks across beams while keeping each beam's private decode tail. Implemented in SGLang and measured on a Qualification Retrieval Platform workload at beam width 200, the combined system raises closed-loop throughput by up to 5.57 times over a custom logit-processor baseline and by up to 2.63 times over BF16 FlashRec.

papers.title: SIMQ: A Single Graph-based Index for Multi-Vector Query
papers.authors: Yifan Lu, Jiabao Jin, Xiaoyao Zhong, Peng Cheng, Xiangyu Wang, Haotian Li, Hua Chen, Junqing Chen, Wei Xi, Heng Tao Shen
papers.abstract: Multi-vector retrieval models such as ColBERT achieve state-of-the-art effectiveness by representing documents as sets of token-level vectors and scoring via MaxSim, but their high computational cost limits scalability to large corpora. Existing approximate methods face fundamental bottlenecks: centroid interaction matrix approaches require computing a full matrix at every query and rely on GPU-accelerated clustering, while data-oblivious compression methods yield unstable recall that requires repeated compensation. We propose SIMQ (Single graph Index for Multi-vector Query), a framework that bridges single-vector graph indices and multi-vector retrieval through data-aware sampling-based clustering and per-token graph navigation, simultaneously bypassing all aforementioned bottlenecks. SIMQ organizes all token vectors into fine-grained clusters via data-aware sampling, builds a single graph index over cluster centroids independently of PLAID's residual representation, and approximates the MaxSim score through per-token graph search without materializing any interaction matrix or relying on GPU acceleration. We provide theoretical analysis showing that, under a manifold assumption and successful cell retrieval, data-aware partitioning has a smaller expected approximation error than a data-oblivious partition. Building on this foundation, SIMQ+ further introduces count-based scoring and a dynamic candidate set to improve robustness across varying query conditions. Experiments on five benchmarks compare recall, throughput, and construction time against several baselines, primarily on CPU; large-scale PLAID k-means centroids are built on a separate GPU machine. SIMQ has been integrated into VSAG, an Ant Group's open-source vector search library.
papers.summary: Multi-vector retrievers represent documents as sets of token-level vectors and score them with MaxSim, which is effective but expensive to scale to large corpora. Existing approximations either materialize a full centroid interaction matrix at every query and rely on GPU clustering, or use data-oblivious compression whose recall is unstable and needs repeated compensation. A single-graph index clusters all token vectors with data-aware sampling, builds one graph over the centroids, and approximates MaxSim by per-token graph search, without materializing an interaction matrix or depending on GPU acceleration. On five benchmarks, at nearly matched recall, the data-aware partition offers comparable or higher query throughput; on SciDocs it reaches 121.6 queries per second, above 105.0 for k-means. The method has been integrated into VSAG, Ant Group's open-source vector search library, so multi-vector retrieval can scale mainly on CPU.

papers.title: KVUse: Reusable-KV User Memory for Efficient LLM Recommenders
papers.authors: Xin Guo, Qiang Zhang, Xiang Zhou, Arushi Rai, Siyu Lin, Yifan Wu, Xiang Shen, Lei Huang, Qunshu Zhang, Xiangjun Fan, Lizhu Zhang
papers.abstract: Memory-augmented recommenders built on large language models (LLMs) maintain a natural-language profile of each user. These profiles are updated by a user profile update path that revises the profile as new interactions arrive and are consumed by downstream task paths like ranking. Because these user profiles are stored as text in the user memory, every ranking LLM call that consumes them must splice them in the prompt and calculate the KV cache of them during the prefill phase. Given these ranking LLM calls are prefill heavy (long prompt but short decoded output) and repeatedly called, these repeated prefill of user profile text dominates the serving. Prefix caching cannot remove it, because these user profiles are preceded by different text in different calls. We present KVUse, which stores the user profiles as reusable key-value (KV) caches instead of text. KVUse trains lightweight LoRA writers by self-distillation, so that the user profile update call produces the reusable KV of the user profile while decoding it, and the LLM can read these reusable KV at new positions and behind new context without recomputation. KVUse also has a customized KV scheduler that uploads the stored reusable KV of the next batch while the current batch is computed, hiding the KV transfer from host memory behind GPU computation. On four InstructRec datasets with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, KVUse shows no statistically significant difference in ranking quality from full prefill over continuous memory update rounds. Under saturated load, KVUse raises the throughput of the downstream scoring path by 4.0x-4.5x and of the profile update path by 1.4x-1.9x.
papers.summary: Memory-augmented recommenders built on large models keep a natural-language profile for each user, then splice it into the prompt and recompute its key-value cache during prefill for every ranking call. Those calls are prefill-heavy, decode-short, and frequent, and prefix caching cannot help because the text before the profile changes from call to call, so repeated prefills dominate serving. One system stores profiles as reusable key-value caches instead of text. Lightweight LoRA writers trained by self-distillation emit that reusable cache while the profile is decoded, and the model can read it at new positions and behind new context without recomputation. A custom scheduler uploads the next batch's stored cache while the current batch runs, hiding host-to-GPU transfer behind compute. On four InstructRec datasets with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, ranking quality shows no statistically significant difference from full prefill. Under saturated load, throughput of the downstream scoring path rises by 4.0 to 4.5 times.

papers.title: CheckCo: Checkpoint-Coordinated Load Balancing for Skewed Event Streams at Scale
papers.authors: Muhammad Anis Uddin Nasir, Reza Sadraei
papers.abstract: Event streams are rarely uniform: a few dominant keys can generate orders of magnitude more events than the rest, overloading the workers that receive them and capping throughput. We present CheckCo, a checkpoint-coordinated load-balancing algorithm built on a dynamic oracle that estimates per-key frequencies from the live stream, with no prior statistics. Workers count events per key locally; at each checkpoint barrier, the counts are merged into a partitioning function that divides each key into a number of splits roughly proportional to its estimated frequency and packs the splits onto workers, and this function routes the next checkpoint window. We derive approximation bounds on the resulting load imbalance from classical scheduling results and bound its total key fan-out. On a production pipeline processing over 100 billion events per day, the most loaded worker receives only 9.8% more events than the average over a day (imbalance ratio 1.10), against 8.03 for key-based routing in simulation; in simulation, CheckCo also needs less than half the fan-out of earlier partitioners that reach comparable balance. Shifts in the key distribution are reflected in routing from the next checkpoint on, and the load stays balanced through job restarts.
papers.summary: Event streams are rarely uniform: a few dominant keys can generate orders of magnitude more events than the rest, overloading the workers that receive them and capping throughput. A checkpoint-coordinated load balancer needs no prior statistics. It estimates per-key frequencies from the live stream: workers count events locally, the counts are merged at each checkpoint barrier, and a partitioning function splits keys in rough proportion to those frequencies, packs the splits onto workers, and routes the next checkpoint window. On a production pipeline processing more than 100 billion events a day, the most loaded worker receives only 9.8% more events than the average over a day, an imbalance ratio of 1.10, against 8.03 for key-based routing in simulation. Shifts in the key distribution are reflected in routing from the next checkpoint, and the load stays balanced through job restarts.

papers.title: SGLang-Neuron v0.1.0: SGLang's Serving Stack on AWS Trainium
papers.abstract: Today we are releasing SGLang-Neuron v0.1.0, the first public release of SGLang’s backend for AWS Trainium.
papers.summary: Serving large language and diffusion models on AWS Trainium inside one stack has lacked a public SGLang backend. The first public preview is a PyTorch-native plugin, co-developed by the SGLang team and Annapurna Labs, and supported during the preview through an AWS Deep Learning Container. Every supported language model shares one fully asynchronous runtime, so chips can run decode steps back to back, and megakernels can run every decoder layer of a step in a single kernel call. Kimi-K3 runs prefill-decode disaggregation across Trainium3 nodes, and GLM-5.2 can serve a million-token context for agentic coding workloads. On GPT-OSS-120B, a host-memory tier for evicted prefixes delivers 72% to 75% more output throughput.

papers.title: SpecSearch: Towards Hardware-Aware Efficient Speculative Decoding
papers.authors: Selin Yildirim, Ali Zeyrek, Deming Chen
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model (LLM) inference, but its optimal configuration depends jointly on workload characteristics, GPU hardware, and available memory. For example, on the RTX~5090, the state-of-the-art speculative drafter DFlash achieves $3.50\times$ the throughput of autoregressive (AR) decoding at low concurrency, but only $0.76\times$ at high concurrency with short outputs. We present SpecSearch, a hardware-aware search engine that jointly optimizes decoding strategy, draft length, and precision across workload--GPU pairs. Its analytical cost model captures memory and compute constraints to identify feasible configurations and narrow the search space for throughput optimization. Guided by this model, calibration measurements are collected from multiple GPUs. Using the measurements, a Jev-based predictor learns to select high-throughput decoding configurations on held-out GPUs without requiring deployment-GPU calibration. The predictor is parameter-efficiently trained on calibration data, while adapting a frozen Qwen3-4B using LoRA adapters and a linear correction layer. Across NVIDIA RTX~5090, H100, L40 and AMD MI300X GPUs, SpecSearch with full calibration achieves an average of $2.01\times$ the throughput of AR and $1.36\times$ the throughput of SD, both served by vLLM. The proposed Jev-based predictor closely matches this search performance with $1.30\times$ throughput improvement over SD with vLLM, while eliminating the need for held-out GPU calibration. Additionally, it retains $97.36\%$ of the throughput achieved by SpecSearch that utilizes full calibration.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding can speed up large-model inference, but the best configuration depends jointly on the workload, the GPU, and available memory. On an RTX 5090, for example, the strong drafter DFlash reaches 3.50 times the throughput of autoregressive decoding at low concurrency, but only 0.76 times at high concurrency with short outputs. A hardware-aware search engine jointly chooses decoding strategy, draft length, and precision for each workload-GPU pair, using an analytical cost model to narrow the feasible set before calibration measurements on multiple GPUs. Across the RTX 5090, H100, L40, and AMD MI300X, full calibration reaches on average 2.01 times the throughput of autoregressive decoding and 1.36 times that of speculative decoding, both served by vLLM. A parameter-efficient predictor closely matches this search on unseen GPUs without requiring calibration on the deployment card.

papers.title: VisHead-Spec: Head-Routed Visual Attention for Multimodal Speculative Decoding
papers.authors: Xin Guo, Arushi Rai, Xiang Zhou, Qiang Zhang, Siyu Lin, Xiangjun Fan, Lizhu Zhang
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates vision-language models(VLMs) while preserving the target model's outputs, but its speedup diminishes under high concurrency serving as the system becomes more compute bounded as the batch size increases. This problem is pronounced for multimodal speculative decoding as the long range of the image tokens in the prompt can significantly increase the computational cost during draft token prediction. The block-diffusion drafters (e.g. DFlash, DSpark) can effectively speed up the draft model efficiency by predicting multiple draft tokens in one forward pass, but their speedup for VLMs under high concurrency is still modest (<9%). In order to understand this gap, we examine the information flow between different modalities from target model to draft model and identify the sparsity pattern of visual attention between the target and draft models: only small set of key-value heads in the draft model need direct visual feature attention in the context and only visual features from top level layers in the target model need to be attended in the context. We therefore propose VisHead-Spec, which selects a small, fixed set of key-value (KV) heads to attend to all image features from top level layers in the target model and restricts the remaining heads to text features. On Qwen3-VL-8B and MMSpec, VisHead-Spec-8 lets 8 of the drafter's 40 KV heads read the image while keeping accepted length within 0.3% of the block-diffusion draft model baseline (i.e. DSpark). At batch size 64, its throughput gain over autoregressive decoding increases to 16.0%, compared with 9.5% for DSpark; at batch size 1, its speedup remains comparable to DSpark.
papers.summary: Speculative decoding can speed up vision-language models while preserving the target model's outputs, but the gain shrinks under high-concurrency serving as the system becomes compute-bound, and long image tokens in the prompt make draft prediction more expensive. Block-diffusion drafters often add only modest speedup for these models at high concurrency. Looking at information flow from the target to the draft model shows a sparse visual-attention pattern: only a small set of draft key-value heads need to read image features, and only from the target model's top layers. A head-routing method therefore lets a fixed subset of heads attend to those top-level image features, and restricts the rest to text. On Qwen3-VL-8B, accepted length stays within 0.3% of the block-diffusion baseline. At a larger batch size, throughput over autoregressive decoding rises to 16.0%, compared with 9.5% for the baseline drafter.

papers.title: TAILROLL: Tail-Aware Rollout Acceleration for RL-Based LLM Post-Training
papers.authors: Niloofar Gholipour, Marcos Assuncao, Timothy Yu, Gursimran Singh, Rajkumar Buyya, Julien Gascon-Samson, Zhenan Fan, Yong Zhang
papers.abstract: RL post-training of large language models (LLMs) is bottlenecked by rollout: heavy-tailed responses leave engines idle as each step waits for the longest response. Asynchronous training masks, but does not eliminate, idle time. We distinguish imbalance waste (uneven placement and decode contention) from straggler waste (waiting for the longest response). Tail length, not average load, often sets the step bound. We propose TAILROLL, an online scheduler integrated into an open-source RL framework. It combines stateless in-flight migration and sufficiency-gated termination. Migration moves decoding requests between engines at chunk boundaries and resumes them with one re-prefill under a freeness-based, cost-aware tail-balancing policy. Termination stops a response when its GRPO group has enough completed samples for advantage estimation, masking its partial output from the training loss. Across ten configurations, TAILROLL reduces rollout bubble ratio by 21% to 74% and cross-engine KV-cache imbalance by 44% to 79%. In end-to-end RL training, it cuts rollout time by 24% to 34%, full step time by 21% to 22% on long-CoT RL, and p95 request latency by 28% to 37%, while raising generation throughput by up to 33% with comparable or higher final reward.
papers.summary: Reinforcement-learning post-training of large models is often bottlenecked by rollout: heavy-tailed responses leave engines idle while each step waits for the longest sequence. Asynchronous training can mask idle time but does not remove it, and tail length, not average load, often sets the step bound. An online scheduler combines stateless in-flight migration with ending a response once enough samples are in. It moves decode requests between engines at chunk boundaries and resumes them with one re-prefill, and it stops a response once its group has enough completed samples for advantage estimation, masking the partial output from the training loss. In end-to-end training, rollout time drops by 24% to 34%, and generation throughput rises by up to 33%, with comparable or higher final reward.

papers.title: TokenRouter: Efficient Serving System for Token-Level LLM Routing
papers.authors: Tianyu Fu, Tengxuan Liu, Ruoxi Wang, Yixin Dong, Yi Ge, Yichen You, Yu Wang
papers.abstract:
Large language model (LLM) routing distributes inference work across different models, advancing the cost-quality Pareto frontier of LLM serving. While coarse-grained routing at the session or query level has been widely adopted in production systems, recent algorithmic work shows that fine-grained token-level routing can yield substantial efficiency and quality gains. However, efficiently serving token-level routed inference poses significant challenges to existing systems. Built on single-LLM assumptions, current systems suffer from severe step desynchronization and frequent batch admission delays under token-level routing, and they also impose high implementation complexity on developers. To address these challenges, we design TokenRouter, an efficient and developer-friendly serving system for token-level routed LLM inference. TokenRouter follows the principle of request-centric programming, model-centric execution: developers describe routing logic from the perspective of a single request, while the runtime launches a subserver for each LLM and dispatches requests asynchronously. Each subserver employs a delayed-batching scheduler, whose optimal hyperparameters are derived from a mathematical throughput model of the system. Across diverse routing algorithms, workloads, and model pairs, TokenRouter achieves 2.01-64.15$\times$ higher decoding throughput than existing systems, substantially advancing the serving efficiency of token-level LLM routing.
Our code is available at https://github.com/thu-nics/TokenRouter.
papers.summary: Routing spreads inference work across different models and can push the cost-quality frontier of serving. Coarse routing at the session or query level is already common in production, and algorithmic work shows that token-level routing can add substantial efficiency and quality gains, but existing serving systems struggle to run it well. Built on single-model assumptions, they suffer step desynchronization and batch-admission delays under token-level routing, and they impose high implementation complexity. A serving system designed for this setting lets developers describe routing logic from the perspective of a single request, while the runtime launches a subserver for each model and dispatches requests asynchronously. Each subserver uses delayed batching whose hyperparameters come from a mathematical throughput model. Across routing algorithms, workloads, and model pairs, decoding throughput is 2.01 to 64.15 times higher than on existing systems, which finally makes token-level routing practical at the serving layer.

papers.title: Keep or Preempt? Termination-Aware Scheduling for LLM Serving with Speculative Decoding
papers.authors: Ziyu Cheng, Mingyan Li, Songtao Guo, Chang Han, Hongyu Xu, Xu Luo
papers.abstract:
Efficient inference is critical for interactive large language model (LLM) serving, where both time-to-first-token (TTFT) and end-to-end (E2E) latency shape user experience. 
Speculative decoding has emerged as a promising solution that reduces inference latency by employing lightweight drafting and parallel verification. However, it introduces a new scheduling issue, i.e., traditional shortest remaining processing time (SRPT) scheduling based on output length estimation becomes less reliable due to its paradigm shift in inference structure.
In this paper, we explore the preemption mechanism of speculative decoding-based LLM serving systems and show that — besides the output length, a request's remaining service time depends on draft acceptance and the number of verification rounds. Building on this insight, we develop a novel termination-aware scheduling framework, named AlmostDone, which first *identifies requests that are almost done* within several future local decoding steps. 
It achieves this by introducing a lightweight predictor built from runtime draft-and-verify states, which helps approximate the SRPT-like scheduling better than existing approaches. Then, AlmostDone *determines whether preemption is worthwhile* through a switching-aware online policy to limit excessive running-set alterations.
papers.summary: Interactive large-model serving is shaped by both time-to-first-token and end-to-end latency. Speculative decoding reduces latency with a lightweight draft and parallel verification, but it also makes classic SRPT scheduling from output-length estimates less reliable: remaining service time also depends on draft acceptance and the number of verification rounds. A termination-aware scheduler first uses a lightweight predictor built from runtime draft-and-verify states to identify requests that will finish within the next few decode steps. It then applies a switching-aware online policy to decide whether preemption is worthwhile, so the running set is not rewritten too often. On an open-source vLLM serving system, it cuts mean time-to-first-token by up to 3.83 times versus the default schedulers, and still achieves up to 2.0 times lower mean time-to-first-token against an oracle length-based preemption baseline.
